title: Wollo famine
summary: Drought and a harvest failure in 1972-73 produced famine in Ethiopia's Wollo province, which killed between 40,000 and 80,000 people according to estimates by Seaman and Holt cited by Human Rights Watch; the Ethiopian Nutrition Institute's 200,000 is called over-pessimistic. Haile Selassie's government tried to conceal the famine. Its exposure by Jonathan Dimbleby helped bring down his rule and led to the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission.

uncertainty.note: HRW dates the famine 1972-3; Miller and Holt describe the 1973 famine after failed 1972 rains, with the crisis peaking in August 1973.

where.modern_name: Dessie, South Wollo, Amhara Region, Ethiopia (proxy pin for Wollo province)
where.historical_name: Wollo province, Ethiopian Empire; Dessie was the provincial capital

importance.justification: The famine and its cover-up contributed to the downfall of Haile Selassie and led to the creation of the Relief and Rehabilitation Commission.

audience_note: Describes a famine with tens of thousands of deaths and a government cover-up; the death estimates are contested.

sources.title: Rebellion and Famine in the North under Haile Selassie (Human Rights Watch report, chapter 3)
The Ethiopian famine
sources.publisher: Cambridge University Press (Proceedings of the Nutrition Society)
sources.author: D. S. Miller and J. F. J. Holt

reviewer_note: The death toll is contested: 40,000-80,000 (Seaman and Holt, via HRW) against 200,000 (Ethiopian Nutrition Institute, said by HRW to rest on over-pessimistic assumptions); Miller and Holt note the lack of definitive data. The pin is Dessie as a proxy for the province, and HRW names it as provincial capital in the text. Miller and Holt supply the 1973 year, the failed rains and the Wollo setting.
